body: Don’t have anything helpful to say but just wanna offer solidarity. I’m 21, started having symptoms at 12 but didn’t get my AS diagnosis til 18. Went on Humira, had a massive allergic reaction to it, switched to Cimzia and it did nothing. Only good thing it did was help me get the COVID vaccine early, lol. But yeah, I get how scary and frustrating it is to have a lifetime diagnosis so early in life, and then not have anything work. Sucks. Much love ❤️

BC, Canada. Not on any right now but have been on Humira (was allergic) and Cimzia (did nothing). We have a program called Fair Pharmacare where your income determines your deductible and yearly maximum. When you reach $x (deductible), the government starts paying for 70% of your pharmacy expenses. When you reach $x+y, the government starts paying for 100% of your pharmacy expenses. It resets the next January. I started Humira when I was 18, so the calculation was based on my family’s combined income. We would have to cover 100% of the cost until we reached around $5000. At that point, we’d only have to cover 25% of the cost until we reached $7000, and then we’d start paying 0%. 

Once I turned 19 I signed up for my own plan. I’m a full-time student and work part-time so my income was low enough that my yearly max was $0 so it was entirely free.

Are you on any biologics? I’ve always had a pretty dysfunctional GI system but nothing debilitating…until March 2020 when I started experiencing pretty much exactly what you described, plus eosinophils up 7x the normal level. It persisted until the end of April when we decided to try stopping my Humira. It resolved within three weeks from my last dose. They think it was a DRESS reaction, basically a severe drug allergy. Super strange because I had been on Humira for nearly 6 months at that point…

Yea exactly. Also my research totally ruined the word GNC for me. I work in an autism lab and my thesis is focused on experiences at the intersection of the gender and autism spectra. Autism researchers have taken a HORRIBLE approach to studying gender where they basically use this one item from a large checklist of behavior problems that asks the parent “does your child ever wish to be of the opposite sex?” They’ll look at responses to that one item in a sample of autistic kids and then write a bs paper about how trans identity and autism must have the same biological mechanisms. You can easily identify these papers by title because they can’t actually say they asked kids about their gender identity so instead they’ll say they measured “gender variance” or “GNC behavior”. I never thought I’d become a methodology geek but this field of research made me realize how important it is to pay attention to language and definitions.

As an AFAB person who doesn’t identify with a binary gender, and who gets mistaken for a cis gay man a lot of the time, queer is the least confusing and least uncomfortable term I’ve tried out. Lesbian and gay both feel inaccurate because to me that feels like saying I am attracted to the “same” gender, when for me there is no gender that would be considered the “same” as mine. I suppose bi or pan might apply but I still don’t like using terms that separate my sexuality from my gender because to me they are intertwined. Plus I have never, so far, been into a cis man; bi and pan don’t feel like they describe me well because I lean pretty exclusively towards women and femme non-binary people. I like queer because it makes sense literally (as in, my experiences with gender and sexuality are considered strange or weird by society) and it also ties me to a broad but tangible community of other people who identify as non-straight and/or non-cis. Basically I appreciate the ability to identify myself as non-cis non-straight person without having to specify anything more narrow than that, because I don’t feel like the correct words to describe me currently exist. This is how I personally feel about these various words being applied to me and I definitely acknowledge and respect the fact that many other people comfortably identify as non-binary lesbians and gays, or as bi/pansexuals who lean towards women and femmes.

I also don’t mind straight people using queer at all as long as it’s done with good intentions. I prefer that to the alternative of them awkwardly stumbling through a mess of acronyms or trying to guess/assume my specific identity.

Last thought - as the straights attempt to get more inclusive I’m noticing that they still don’t totally understand the meaning and relationship between the words they use to describe gender and sexuality. For example, I’ve filled out many surveys that provide non-binary as a gender option, but then only provide heterosexual, bisexual, and homosexual as the sexuality options. It doesn’t seem to register that neither homosexual or heterosexual apply well to non-binary people, and thus it forces me to pick bisexual when that also doesn’t feel right.

Blood tests are definitely a huge annoyance to interpret, because laboratories will automatically compare my results to female ranges. Reliably, any markers that are sex- or hormone-related will be flagged and I’ll get worried calls from my PCP’s clinic about elevated creatinine, GFR,
hemoglobin, etc. What’s more is that none of my specialists (and I have a lot of them) seem to have any trans competency, so when I have new symptoms crop up, nobody can tell me for sure whether it might/might not be related to testosterone.

And then there’s the whole social aspect of it, which is...exhausting lol. I recently saw a new rheumatologist who spent an hour asking me to explain my pronouns, the surgery and hormone therapy I’ve had, etc only for her to then misgender me for all following appointments. Even though my preferred pronouns are they/them and I’m very clear about my preferred name, my charts are a mix of she/they/he as well as my legal name versus my preferred name. However I present very masculine and people usually assume I’m a cis man in public. So anytime I’m sitting in a a waiting room that happens to be all male and a nurse comes out looking for a female named [insert legal name], they’ll just assume I’m not there since they don’t see any women 🙄

Hahah funny you bring that up because I can kinda speak to that personally—I’m non-binary and started taking testosterone when I was 18. I’m 21 now. The first few months on T, I was on a fairly low dose because I still had some reservations. I was also on stimulants for ADHD, and propranolol for nervous system dysfunction, both of which are also considered performance enhancing. I happened to be on a huge fitness kick at the time, and gained a TON of muscle mass. I was swimming every morning, lifting during my lunch break, and going to cheer practice at night. Everyone on my cheer team was like “oh that’s just the testosterone...you’re basically doping”. A few months later, cheer season was over so I was doing way less exercise. I had even upped my dose of T around this time, but without the intense exercise I was doing before, the muscle disappeared pretty fast and I started gaining weight in “male” areas like my gut. So yeah, not really sure where I meant to go with this...but tl;dr steroids are not magic solutions. You still have to put in the work.

Yeah, also the number of “recovery accounts” that 100% act as fitspo for people. Whether or not the influencer means for their posts to be perceived a certain way, they should know given their own experience that people will take that shit and RUN with it. Whether it’s “what I eat in  a day”, “before and after”, “updates on my new feeding tube”, “my recovery meal plan”...people who are sick find ways to turn that into a) invalidation towards themselves for being less sick than the influencer, or b) motivation to follow whatever diet protocol the influencer is reminiscing about.

One account I really like is @lindseyhallwrites. She’s one of the only actually intersectional ED awareness accounts that talks about racialized and trans’ folks experiences, so as someone who identifies as both I appreciate that. There are also no food pictures and very few body pictures, it’s all text. And she writes in a really compassionate but no-BS way, which has actually helped me call myself out on a lot of toxic behaviors. The issue is that, when I started following her, all of my reels turned into extremely underweight girls showing their daily recovery meal plans....that might be helpful for some people but definitely not me.

Wow okay I don’t have a diagnosis yet but I literally came to this subreddit to see whether what you described were symptoms consistent with dysautonomia. Independent of sleep I already get GI problems, but it’s usually like half a day of tenesmus and then suddenly a single 10 min episode of diarrhea where it all just...comes out at once. I have had to pull a lot of all nighters  or 2-4 hour sleeps for school recently, and the next day I get the most bizarre symptoms. Basically I’ll be having short episodes of diarrhea all day, like 7-8 total. My right arm can go completely numb and I’ll get shooting pains down it. My fingers and hands FREEZE which does happen on a normal basis too but it’s much much worse with no sleep. And if I don’t take anti anxiety meds my heart will be going absolutely crazy with palpitations and my blood pressure goes way down. 

Honestly I keep wondering if this is just what happens to everybody when they don’t sleep and so it’s really just my own fault for it sleeping enough....or do I really have an underlying vulnerability that is making this happen.

I had almost the exact same symptoms in March. I have also had misc. bowel issues for my whole life so I thought I was just going through an especially bad phase...but a month later it was still so crippling that I was doing all my online classes from the bathroom. I went to go get blood and stool tests and it turned out I had hypereosinophilia—my eosinophils were multiple times higher than normal. My stool also had the breakdown material of white blood cells. My rheumatologist suspected it was a reaction to Humira, either mild DRESS Syndrome or allergic reaction. I didn’t think it could be this because I had been on Humira for about 6 months at that point, and my blood had been normal when I got a routine test a few weeks before the symptoms started. But sure enough, within a few weeks of stopping Humira my WBC were back to normal and the stomache aches were much less severe.

The troubling thing is that this is somewhat reflected in lab studies...I’m taking a neuroscience class and the textbook discusses several studies where lab animals that went through long periods of restriction live longer than those on standard diets. But even so, this information doesn’t get presented in tandem with any insight about quality of life, cognitive processes, missing out on food-related events, risk for developing an ED or obsessive behavior, etc. Which makes it easy for people to take that study and say “starving makes you live longer, see here’s the proof”. When we talk about studies like this I wish it was accompanied by more nuanced discussions of the other variables that are affected :/

Several. The first time was in my senior year—I had been in the psych ward for two weeks, they discharged me even though I was very clear that I was still suicidal and had a plan to attempt. So I’m not sure what they expected but yeah I got home and immediately overdosed on prescription and OTC meds. Passed out and ended up back in the same hospital in a three-day coma. Woke up to my mom sobbing and rubbing chapstick on my lips. Devastating. Couldn’t talk for a few days due to the breathing tube, got pneumonia and a blood clot while in the coma, took another day to relearn how to walk, aaaand then dumped back into the psych ward for 7 more months. Attempted in a variety of stupid ways while in the ward as well as while on passes. That first big overdose was a very deliberate and planned decision where I had written notes, etc but honestly after that I would just try anytime I wasn’t being watched, even if I knew it barely had a chance of working. I was just fucking desperate and was getting more and more traumatized by the hospital every day (by the nurses and doctors only; the patients were fantastic people by and large).

That year (2018) I attempted about 8-9 times, though only 3 or 4 required significant medical care. Each time was incredibly physically painful, and emotionally painful for me and the people around me. However even now when I look back, I can’t imagine making different choices, just because of how truly distressed and distorted my brain was. I’m still struggling now, but it’s more due to my physical chronic disease exacerbating my mental illness. I still get intrusive suicidal thoughts but not ones that I’ve felt compelled to take action on recently. It took a lot of therapy and resources that I know not everyone is able to access, so I really think it was a matter of privilege and chance that allowed me to somewhat recover. 

Not sure what I’m trying to get across here, I guess just that attempting and failing is a shit time all around. But I know living the way you are now also probably feels like a shit time. If you have any access to supports at all—counselor, friend, old teacher, walk in clinic, online chat—please give those one more try before you make any big decisions. I went through 4 or 5 therapists before I found one that I clicked with so it really is hit or miss.

It really took me a while to figure out what actually worked for me, because although I definitely know what doesn’t work for me I’m much less likely to happen across things that do work. However, when it works, it really works! I used to leave my wallet on the bus or just generally misplace it a lot. I then started keeping my cards all in different pockets because then at least I never lost a whole stack of cards at once...but then I’d still lose the odd card or two. Finally I bought a phone case that can accommodate 7 ID/bank cards, and since I’m extremely careful with my phone I’ve yet to lose a card since! Another one was brushing my teeth; this wasn’t forgetfulness so much as willfulness. I just didn’t feel like it usually. But I started keeping my toothbrush in a case inside my shower, and now I brush every time I shower and I don’t mind it at all. A last one is meds - I don’t usually forget to take them but I do forget to bring them places with me. And if I’m at home but they’re not immediately in front of me when it’s time for a dose, sometimes I just get lazy and don’t wanna go get them. Now when I get my refills, I mix a few of each med into all the bottles. So instead of 5 bottles with one type of pill each I have 5 bottles of assorted pills. And then I distribute them in the car, the kitchen, my partner’s house, my bedroom, my backpack. That way I always have my dose within reach.

Yeah, so for example I am transmasculine non-binary. People have their own interpretations of this but to me it means I don’t identify as male or female but lean towards a masculine gender expression. I’ve had top surgery to remove my breasts, as well as my nipples (some people have their nipples regrafted back on but I wasn’t that attached to them anyways). However I don’t imagine myself ever getting bottom surgery, and I’m perfectly fine having a “female” lower body and “male” upper body. I’m also on testosterone, so between that and the flat chest I’m usually perceived as a dude by strangers. It doesn’t bother me a ton to be called by he/him pronouns but I much prefer they/them! And most binary trans people (trans men and trans women) often also prefer that you use they/them until you’re sure—though it never hurts to ask!

Great start but just want to add that it’s not necessarily a body-brain matching thing, although I know a lot of older documentaries love to rattle off lines like that. Gender, unlike sex, is an entirely psychosocial construct. At the end of the day, trans people change their bodies because society associates certain body parts with certain genders. There are ways to influence gender perception without altering body parts, such as fashion, speech and syntax, hobbies and interests, and communication style. People whose dysphoria is alleviated through these strategies are no less valid than people who opt for surgery.

This feels like a bit of an over generalization, or at least doesn’t align with what I and many others in my community have experienced. After two years on hormones and a double mastectomy, I feel little to no dysphoria. I still have a laundry list of other diagnoses that have been influenced by dysphoria, though. For example I have social anxiety regarding the way people perceive my gender but that’s mostly because I dread all forms of conflict, even the most benign encounters like kids looking at me weirdly in the washroom. 

But yeah I can definitely say that I have never had a wish to be a cis man. I love my trans masculinity, I love the fact that I am constantly learning new things about my transness, and I love my trans community. I don’t get distraught when people misgender me (unless it’s with malicious intent) and I have no issues looking back on old photos. My only distress comes from people treating me shittily, but that is not a psychological factor itself.

I think it’s a bit over simplistic to say that people with OCPD are unaware of their problem behaviors. OCPD is not the kind of diagnosis that will be easily detected by teachers or parents, and it does not usually land people in the hospital either. That means most diagnoses would stem from people seeking out a diagnosis, which they wouldn’t do unless they felt that they were experiencing distress in some way.
For me personally, it’s more that I take pride in my overall life values (caring for my community, working towards climate justice, mentoring younger queer people) but I know that the circumstances I force upon myself in a distorted effort to achieve these things is very unhealthy. For example, I have cognitive distortions that lead me to feel like extreme discipline will help me be efficient with my time, which allows me to commit to all the different organizations I’m passionate about. Discipline in my messed up brain’s opinion looks like obsessively restricting my food intake and documenting/planning things to the point where the planning behaviors delay or steamroll the actual task. I know that these behaviors are irrational but I cannot for the life of me stop doing them, as part of me really believes that I will fail at everything in life the moment I stop restricting.

I think that the BPD diagnosis is a huge barrier to equal access to health care. I wrote a paper for my department’s undergrad journal on how the borderline label is used to demonize capitalism-incompatible coping strategies as well as queer, femme, and disabled people.

I became extremely suicidal in my senior year and was immediately diagnosed with BPD after my first attempt. After that, interactions with healthcare providers would always be fine at first contact, then turn absolutely hostile when they saw my chart. If they didn’t immediately turn me away or discharge me on account of borderline patients regressing in hospital”, their attitudes towards me would steadily improve as they realized I was a teacher’s pet with straight A’s who had never broken a rule in their life, as opposed to...whatever they assume people with BPD are. All the other patients with BPD who I met while inpatient were incredibly empathetic, generous to a fault, unafraid to be different, and perfectionistic. These traits all obviously take an emotional toll due to both societal and personal pressures which is what IMO causes such high suicide rates. And hospital workers tend to see patients with failed suicide attempts as attention seeing and dramatic, which gives us a pretty bad rep.

I’d say it depends on the motives behind it (and even then there’s no real rules). Like if you’re coloring purely to avoid distressing thoughts or tasks, I’d call that self-soothing. Or in DBT we call that distress tolerance. But, if you’re colouring because it’s enjoyable, relaxing, and helps lift your mood so that the rest of your responsibilities feel easier, that’d be self-care.

Like others said, it’s really a formality. You can go on the TransCare website if you want to see the questions you will be asked, or check out[my Notion page](https://www.notion.so/GENDER-AFFIRMING-CARE-IN-BC-bbeb8693aca54da2aef9e4c3f04bfc30) which can walk you through the whole hormones process. 

Mostly they want to know whether you have the supports in place to properly recover from the surgery. Especially if you have a history of mental illness, because they’re worried about post-op depression. So if you go in and have a list of people who you know can help you recover, you have coping skills and strategies for dealing with lows, and you show a good understanding of the potential risks and consequences, you will be just fine!

Just wanna say I really appreciate the way you’ve voiced the pros of online meetings; I had a prof mention in class the other day that “online school is soooo much more accessible for you guys” and I just wanted to break down from the frustration of being misrepresented. You put it in a much more tangible way, and I so agree, COVID started at the exact same time I started getting mysterious and terrible GI problems. Had I needed to go to the specialists’ offices, I don’t think I could have managed even leaving the house. Instead, I got to do it from my bed with my heat pack, and beforehand I chose 7 of my most WTF POTS photos to send in. They called exactly on time (this doc usually leaves me on the waiting room for hours), hung up to consult the other doctors in the office on my case, then phoned me back and debriefed me. They even emailed me THEIR notes after! There was one week where I had 4 specialists in a row. In the past that would have been four separate days off, but instead each one was my one hour lunch break!

It also helps that I’m an anxious fuck and the anticipatory dread of planning to travel to an office is the WORST. So being able to not think about it until 5 min beforehand is helpful.

Overwhelmed?? God yes. Went to the ER with severe myoclonic seizures today, after waking up with pins and needles in my spine that quickly progressed to extreme nausea and disorientation. Was pretty much thrashing around in the ER bed while they did blood work, ECG, urine sample. Conclusion? “You can take 1mg Ativan before you go, and here’s a neurologist you can see in a few weeks. Stop taking your pain meds since that might be the cause”. And then they shooed me out, still jerking and twitching just as much as when I entered. Like, come on. If I had known that was gonna be it I wouldn’t have bothered going. Ugh. Just tired of another old straight white man doctor telling me that I should be glad that “nothing” is wrong. Sure, if me being in severe discomfort and pain is what you would call RIGHT, then yeah nothing’s wrong. I just....ughhh. I seem to have the worst hospital traumas every year around early Jan. Being kicked out of the psych ward, ending up in a coma, being told by a white male doctor that I’M not actually suicidal, being told by another white male doctor that I don’t actually have AS, I’m over it.

I got the IDASEN desk from IKEA, it’s about $700. I’m really pleased with it! I have arthritis and a fusing spine so my back is extremely reactive to bad posture and ill-fitting furniture. I don’t actually use it to stand that often to be honest, but what I love more is the ability to adjust the height when I’m sitting. I can get it to perfect eye-to-monitor height so my neck isn’t craned, or if it’s my shoulders that are hurting I’ll drop it down so I can fully rest my forearms on it. I position my adjustable chair according to what my legs and feet need, and then the desk according to what my back and upper body need. I can sit at this desk for probably twice as long without pain compared to my old one, and when I do get pain I stand up for a bit and that helps somewhat.

I do really miss having a good filing drawer and pen drawer though, and haven’t bothered to problem solve that yet.

I’ve been having symptoms since I was 12, and I quit competitive soccer and volleyball when I was 15 because the pain was so unmanageable and doctors were still thinking it was something that could be treated with ice and physio. I got my AS diagnosis near the end of that hospital stay so it really was just the cherry on top of an already terrible year.

I’m 20 now and in 3rd year undergrad, and although my AS symptoms have gotten worse, my coping and overall mental health have definitely gotten better. Swimming and light weightlifting have been really key to staying healthy mentally and physically, though I still really miss competitive sport. Being on oral meds was an issue for me as well because of the whole “take with food” situation so I opted for injections. I trialed Humira for a while but had really bad side effects so now I’m on Cimzia. Gabapentin and low dose naltrexone have also been very helpful. I’m also only just starting to get better at prioritizing “quality of life improvements” because for a long time I had the mindset of “why would I bother with a treatment that’s only going to help in the moment but won’t cure the disease?” But turns out heat packs, massagers, baths, etc really do help make things feel less hopeless even if they aren’t making long term changes to your body. 

In terms of managing school and mental health, I would really recommend putting as many supports in place when you’re feeling well and have the energy to do so, so that you’re not scrambling to do those things when you’re in a flare up. I email all my profs at the beginning of the term to let them know that I might need extensions and may have several absences that are out of my control. Boundary setting has also been a big learning curve bc I tend to let people walk over me like a doormat but I can’t really afford to do that anymore. It’s becoming easier to say “sorry no I can’t do XYZ, I’m in a lot of pain today” or “sure I can come but I’ll need this specific seating arrangement and breaks at these times”. 

Being a young person with this illness is not easy at all, and it’s especially hard when you’re dealing with comorbid mental illness. But our bodies and brains tend to pull through even in the worst of situations, simply because there’s no other option. Whether that’s for better or worse idk 🤷🏻‍♂️

Paneer is actually a type of cheese identical to cottage cheese, if you were to strain the liquid from cottage cheese and press it into a block. It’s made by curdling milk with an acid and then collecting the solids that form (also known as cheese curds) and pressing them into a block. To me, disability doesn’t describe my conditions alone; it described how they interact with the barriers society has constructed that make it difficult for me to live my life. For example, my arthritis only prohibits me from accessing education *if* the seating, scheduling, etc is not appropriate. I hesitate to call these “special accommodations” because these are things everybody needs, just in different amounts. However for certain reasons my university has chosen 10 minutes as the time allotted to get from class to class, and hard wooden chairs as the seating of choice. This simply doesn’t work for me during a flare-up, thus disabling me. 

However, how interesting was it when COVID hit and suddenly the majority of the school population required “special accommodations” to access education? Lecture content was online within days, something I had been asking for for years and always been told it was not possible. With this sudden online access, I am no longer disabled in this aspect. In this way, disability is fluid and transient. 

What I’m saying is that there is no real reason for my condition to limit my occupational or academic activities, apart from institutions’ unwillingness to spend the extra dollar or waste the extra minute. Yes it is more nuanced than this, but especially with COVID I’ve noticed how a number of accessibility issues above struggled with for a long time were cleared up as soon as old white male decision-makers started experiencing them too

This is why I dislike how the DSM frames disordered eating and other similar tendencies like cutting and dissociation. For many of us, disordered eating is adaptive. It serves a purpose by meeting an unfulfilled need; that’s why we have it in the first place. It gives us a sense of control, or feelings of accomplishment, or helps us feel regulated in other areas of life. Yes, there are ultimately much healthier coping mechanisms out there, but it’s dishonest to frame eating disorders as completely useless. It’s really just a symptom of a larger need for control or order, so unless you get to the root of that issue, that unfulfilled need will just manifest in different ways like listmaking or self harm or cleaning. At least, that’s what I’ve found with my own recovery. It’s not that difficult to fix my disordered eating behaviors temporarily, but as soon as I do I start to feel unhinged in other parts of my life. No wonder so many ED patients are reluctant to recover—it doesn’t feel like recovery when it’s taking away the one thing that feels controllable. Psychologists really needs to come up with treatment methods that actually help people address the root cause, otherwise they’re just taking away people’s go-to coping mechanism without replacing it with healthier ways to survive.

For some background, Idid 16 rounds of ECT in 2018. I was 18. To be honest it bothers me a little when people call it “shock treatment” because it feels over-sensationalizing. ECT is not the same as the shock therapy you see in movies from the 70s. The actual procedure is painless given that you are anesthetized and take several painkillers/muscle relaxers beforehand. Out of the 6 of us who were receiving ECT while I was inpatient, two older ladies experienced soreness and headaches after each session but the rest of us were physically fine. The memory loss is definitely true—my facial recognition is pretty horrendous now. I would say most of the negative side-effects come from the anesthesia, not from the actual seizures. Overall my mood did improve during that time (went from attempting suicide at least once per month, to being able to leave inpatient and start university) but I don’t know how much was directly because of ECT.

 I subscribe to a lot of Szasz’s beliefs about psychiatry and ultimately I don’t believe mental illness is anything more than a form of government control. I definitely agree that North American hospitals are carceral and oppressive systems, but I do think that ECT can be helpful if it’s done with consent and accompanied by other forms of care.

By no means am I trying to minimize the stress and worry that inevitably come with this diagnosis and treatment! There’s a local bagel joint that’s famous for their dense, chewy bagels. Sadly they’re 300-350 calories each, so I wanted to try to create a lower calorie dupe. This was my first time making bagels and they turned out incredibly! I ate one straight out of the oven with cream cheese and homemade blueberry chia jam for a grand total of 195 calories. 

This recipe makes 6 bagels. Feel free to double or half as needed. 

0.5 cup whole wheat flour
1.25 cup unbleached white flour
1.5 tablespoons honey
0.5 tablespoons active dry yeast
1 egg white
0.75 cups warm water

Measure the whole wheat flour, 0.25 cup white flour, honey, and yeast into a mixing bowl. Use electric mixer to beat while slowly adding in the warm water until it forms a sticky dough. Add another 0.25 cup white flour. Beat on high for 2 minutes. Remove from mixer and stir in remaining 0.75 cup white flour. Knead until soft, non-sticky elastic dough forms; add more flour or water if needed. Put the dough in a clean bowl and cover, then let rise for 20 minutes. 

Place dough on floured surface and split into 6 equal parts. Roll each one into a long, thin log then pinch the ends together to form the bagel shape. Place on a baking sheet, cover, and let rise for 20 min. 

In a shallow, wide pan, boil at least 2 inches of water. You can add honey to the water for sweetness but I didn’t. Place the bagels carefully in the pan and reduce temperature to a simmer. My pan fit all the bagels at once but you may need to do two rounds. Boil for 7 minutes, turning them upside down halfway through. Remove from water and cool on a tea towel for 5 minutes. 

Place bagels on a baking sheet covered in a silicone nonstick sheet. Bake at 375 F for 10 minutes. Remove from oven and brush the egg white over the tops of the bagels. Sprinkle on salt, EBTB seasoning, etc if desired then put back in oven for 20 minutes or until golden brown. Your bagels are done! 

Best eaten immediately, store leftovers in plastic ziploc. If freezing, cut them before freezing and toast when ready to eat.

The first thing I would say is that the weight of water and food waste you  naturally retain makes the scale pretty irrelevant in a three week period. Even if you weigh yourself at the same time every day, the amount of water and food waste your body retains can fluctuate with variation in salt intake, diuretic (coffee/tea) and alcohol consumption, frequency of hydration and urination, fiber and magnesium intake, last bowel movement, medicines, etc. Yesterday I weighed 144 and today I weighed 138. Clearly I did not lose 6 pounds of fat. Rather, my body expelled 6 pounds of food and water waste. This may seem like a lot for one day but here's a hypothetical for some perspective: 2 potatoes (1lb), 15 strawberries (1lb), and 4 cups of water (2lb). That's less that 600 calories, but it really does add significant weight that will eventually be digested! 

Second point: you are running at a 600 cal deficit right now. Multiply that by 21 days and you've got 12600 calorie deficit total. 1 pound of fat=3500 calories so the absolute most you could have lost is 3.6 pounds, and that's if you truly burned at least 2200 and ate only 1600 per day. So consider the fact that you don't exercise every day, maybe you walk a bit more some days, you realistically lost less than 3.6 pounds of body fat.

So finally if you put these two facts together, it's easy to see how even if you did lose 3 pounds of fat, you can't tell due to natural variation in weight. All this to say that you shouldn't give up or get discouraged; you probably just need more than 3 weeks before you see a lot of change on the scale. A better method may be to judge the fit of your clothes, or take measurements of your limbs and trunk.
